rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prevalent view identifies the oath's agents as angels taking believers' souls gently and unbelievers' harshly, but Islahi says its reports are unsound and unsupported by the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: the dominant opinion is that they refer to angels who claim the souls of the disbelievers harshly and those of the believers gently

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic oaths principally bear witness to a claim; the sworn object need not itself be sacred or blessed.
rows.anchor: generally the oaths that occur in the Qur’ ān are meant to bear witness to a premise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads the first oath as forceful winds that uproot trees, houses, and other things firmly rooted in the earth.
rows.anchor: is used for strong winds which uproot trees and houses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links the wind's uprooting force to the storm sent against ʿĀd and connects the verb used there to the term in this verse.
rows.anchor: On a day of unremitting woe, We had let loose on them a howling wind which plucked out the people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nashitat describes gentle, mild winds, as in the corresponding expression in al-Dhāriyāt.
rows.anchor: has been used to mean gentle and mild winds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Dhāriyāt mentions gentle wind before rain, while this sūrah mentions wind independently, encompassing beneficial and destructive effects.
rows.anchor: Here the wind is mentioned independently because of which it can include both its good and bad effects

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind's life-giving and destructive effects are both under God's control; the Moses and Pharaoh account illustrates that even a gentle wind can destroy.
rows.anchor: even gentle winds can become a source of destruction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabihat means floating and, in context, describes clouds because clouds and winds are closely connected.
rows.anchor: Contextual indications point to the fact that it is used as an attribute of the clouds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following two attributes apply to the clouds; the particle fa marks both that relation and their sequence.
rows.anchor: the two attributes mentioned subsequently begin with the particle ف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath depicts cloud-bearing winds racing over divinely assigned regions and carrying out God's orders by bringing rain or destruction.
rows.anchor: at some places, they send down rain as a blessing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The racing image depicts groups of clouds appearing in the sky as if competing to fulfill their assigned duty first.
rows.anchor: various groups of clouds appear and try to outrun one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath's complement is omitted because the following account supplies it; its sense is that what people are promised will certainly occur.
rows.anchor: what you are being promised with is certain to come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wind and cloud signs warn Quraysh that God's threatened punishment is easy for Him to bring and that stronger nations were destroyed by winds.
rows.anchor: the arrogant leaders of Quraysh are warned that the punishment they are being threatened with should not be regarded as impossible

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–14 depict the eternal punishment of Judgment first; the worldly punishment for rejecting messengers is an additional arrangement.
rows.anchor: The punishment of the Day of Judgement is mentioned first because it is this punishment which everyone should remain aware of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The upheaval's inner effects are fearful, beating hearts and downcast eyes; people who feared the Day without seeing it will be safe from its pangs.
rows.anchor: Many a heart on that day will be beating and the eyes will be downcast because of fear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart is the person's real self, and the eyes are linked to it because they reveal its most concealed thoughts.
rows.anchor: eyes reflect the most concealed thoughts of the heart

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers mock resurrection by asking whether they will return to their original state after becoming decayed bones.
rows.anchor: when they are warned that they will be re-created after death so that they can be made accountable for their deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated interrogative expresses their escalating amazement: resurrection is strange, and resurrection after bodily decay seems even stranger to them.
rows.anchor: further amazement on their part

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their claim that return would mean grave loss is spoken mockingly yet also betrays their inner fear and awareness that the arguments carry weight.
rows.anchor: these words reflect their inner-selves: their hearts were not satisfied on denying the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers defer concern for Judgment, reasoning they will deal with its grave danger if it ever arrives rather than make life miserable now.
rows.anchor: they would tackle it when it would come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A single shout, the second trumpet blast, will raise people from their graves and gather them immediately on the broad field of resurrection.
rows.anchor: The single shout refers to the second sound of the trumpet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sāhira means a level, broad expanse and here denotes the gathering field.
rows.anchor: means “a level and wide expanse of ground.” Here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Judgment's punishment, the passage turns to historical proof that rejecting God's messengers brings punishment in this world; Moses is chosen as especially famous evidence.
rows.anchor: The previous paragraph portrays the punishment of the Day of Judgement. These verses depict historical evidence to substantiate it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular address in ‘Has Moses's story reached you?’ can address people generally, and the account compresses every lesson-relevant phase from his call to Pharaoh's drowning.
rows.anchor: the singular pronoun present in these words address the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's transgression included claiming divinity; Moses was first to invite him gently to reform and then warn him of his fate.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh claimed himself to be the great God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Do you desire to reform yourself?’ combines great affection with the majesty expected of God's envoy, while leaving Pharaoh an opening to accept guidance.
rows.anchor: it simultaneously has great affection and also great majesty which should be the hallmark of an envoy of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tazakka refers broadly to a life free of egotism, selfishness, and oppression, characteristic of those who fear God.
rows.anchor: It refers to a life which is without egotism, selfishness and oppression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets aim to purify people's inner selves through God's books; Moses offers Pharaoh this same reform and guidance toward God.
rows.anchor: the real objective of the prophets of God has always been to purify the inner-selves of people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses reminds Pharaoh that virtuous life grows from fear of God, and fear rests on true comprehension of God.
rows.anchor: a virtuous life emanates from the fear of God and this fear itself has its roots in the true comprehension of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses's staff becoming a snake was the great sign; apart from the white hand, the other miracles were concealed in and manifested through it.
rows.anchor: except for the miracle of the white hand all other miracles were concealed in it and manifested themselves through it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even after witnessing the miracle, Pharaoh denied Moses's message, calling him a magician and a liar.
rows.anchor: and dubbed him as a magician and a liar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh turned away and plotted to defeat Moses by arranging a contest with Aaron and expert magicians; his advisers warned ordinary magicians risked defeat.
rows.anchor: it would be better if expert magicians were called up from all parts of the empire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh repeatedly promised to accept Moses's demand if calamities were lifted, then broke his word, increasing Moses's influence among the Copts.
rows.anchor: repeated breaches were instrumental in increasing the influence of Moses (sws) on the Copts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Pharaoh's expanded speech, he boasts of Egypt's sovereignty and rivers and disparages Moses before his people.
rows.anchor: Do not the sovereignty of Egypt and these rivers which flow beneath my feet belong to me?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's speech also asks why gold ornaments or angels did not accompany Moses; it befools his disobedient people before God drowns them.
rows.anchor: He was able to befool his people through this speech and they were in fact a people disobedient

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's exemplary punishment included drowning in this world and consigning him to Hell in the next.
rows.anchor: the Almighty seized him in the punishment of this world and that of the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses account primarily addresses Quraysh: the wise learn from others' fate instead of waiting for calamity to strike them.
rows.anchor: they should learn a lesson from this tale

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky's complexity and signs of power invite people who doubt recreation to reflect on God's grandeur and ability.
rows.anchor: Some great aspects of God’s power and wisdom found in the sky are referred to here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky's initial night was smoke; God later uncovered light and ordered night and day, showing that recreating mankind is no harder for Him.
rows.anchor: initially there was night all over within the sky

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky's complexity and providential order show God's power to recreate people and need to hold them accountable, answering denial and establishing Judgment's wisdom.
rows.anchor: not only an answer has been given to the objection raised by the rejecters of the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth's water, fodder, and mountains display God's power and providence, showing He can easily recreate people.
rows.anchor: attention is directed to the signs found on the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If worldly life were only eating, drinking, and dying, the world would be a place of merry-making and its Creator unjustly deemed unwise.
rows.anchor: this world is a place of merry-making

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth's water, fodder, mountains, and provision for people and cattle display God's power and providence; this nourishment implies accountability, not a merely hedonistic life.
rows.anchor: The Almighty did not merely provide for the needs of man, He has also catered for the needs of the cattle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent order of earth and sky raises a question against 41:11, which says the sky was vapor after earth's creation; Islahi directs readers to his earlier explanation.
rows.anchor: was the sky created after the earth?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky and earth are like a building whose roof and floor are planned together; differing creation descriptions can refer to different phases, with earth receiving final touches later, while God alone knows all phases.
rows.anchor: The sky is the roof of this building and the earth is its floor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Today people are heedless of their actions and mock warnings, but the Day's arrival will restore their senses.
rows.anchor: when he is warned of that day, he makes fun of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Judgment arrives, man will regain his senses and see what he earned in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: when that day arrives, he will come to his senses and see what he has earned in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell will be unveiled for those destined to face it and already stand ready behind a veil; God's servants who feared it unseen are kept away and do not hear it.
rows.anchor: only the veil will need to be lifted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘Hell shall be his abode’ emphasizes that transgressors will remain in Hell forever with no other place to go.
rows.anchor: they will abide in Hell forever

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who fear facing God resist running after worldly life and curb their base desires.
rows.anchor: those who feared facing the Almighty and instead of running after this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited description of Judgment as a day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds explains what it means to fear standing before God.
rows.anchor: The day when men will rise to stand up before the Lord of the worlds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear of standing before God restrains a person from base desires; without that fear, nothing stops pursuit of them.
rows.anchor: It is the fear of this encounter with the Almighty which stops a person from following his base desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is assured that the questioners tease him about when Judgment will arrive, while his responsibility is to warn and give the heedful a chance to prepare.
rows.anchor: the only responsibility of the Prophet (sws) was to inform people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ayān asks when a future event occurs, not where; marṣāhā's port and anchoring image makes the question sarcastic.
rows.anchor: it would be erroneous to translate it as “where;”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God knows Judgment's time; the Prophet is not charged with announcing it, so questioners should leave the matter to God.
rows.anchor: no one except the Almighty has knowledge of this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's warning benefits those who fear Judgment on the basis of arguments before seeing it; he is not responsible for those demanding to witness it first.
rows.anchor: his warnings will only affect those who believe in and fear this Day in the light of arguments even though they have not seen it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Judgment, people will see that their worldly stay seemed no longer than an evening or morning, so its arrival should not be dismissed as distant.
rows.anchor: more than the first or last part of a day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not pursue the arrogant at the cost of his own companions.
rows.anchor: So he must not go after them at the cost of his own companions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an is God's reminder and authoritative command; people who refuse it face consequences, and its noble bearers deserve honor rather than indulgence of arrogant opponents.
rows.anchor: It is an authoritative word of God which commands obedience; it is not the request of a supplicant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage reminds the arrogant deniers of Judgment of the phases of human life and the possibility of re-creation.
rows.anchor: various phases of their life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Creator's system of provision for people and animals shows that He will call them to account; success belongs to those who fulfill their duties toward His favors.
rows.anchor: the Being who has made such an elaborate arrangement to nourish and nurture people will never leave them unaccountable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgment leaves people absorbed in themselves and unconcerned with relatives; the fearful will rejoice, while the indifferent face gloom and misfortune.
rows.anchor: people on that day will be so engrossed in their own affairs that they will become unconcerned with their near ones
